related_questions.question: What are the new rules for Roth IRAs?

text_blocks.snippet: For 2025, individuals can contribute up to $7,000 to a Roth IRA, or $8,000 if they are age 50 or older. The ability to contribute the full amount depends on income, with single filers needing a modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) below $150,000 and those married filing jointly needing a MAGI below $236,000, according to NerdWallet. If your income is higher, you may be able to make partial contributions or be ineligible to contribute at all, according to Fidelity and Vanguard.

list.title: Single Filers:
list.snippet: MAGI below $150,000 for full contribution, with reduced contributions possible between $150,000 and $165,000, notes NerdWallet.

list.title: Married Filing Jointly:
list.snippet: MAGI below $236,000 for full contribution, with reduced contributions possible between $236,000 and $246,000, according to Vanguard.

list.title: Ineligibility:
list.snippet: Single filers with a MAGI of $165,000 or more and those married filing jointly with a MAGI of $246,000 or more cannot contribute to a Roth IRA, says Fidelity.

list.title: Spousal IRAs:
list.snippet: A non-working spouse can contribute to a Roth IRA through a spousal IRA, provided the working spouse has enough earned income.

list.title: MAGI:
list.snippet: Modified Adjusted Gross Income is used to determine eligibility. It's your AGI with certain deductions added back in, according to Investopedia.

list.title: Deadline:
list.snippet: The deadline for Roth IRA contributions is typically April 15th of the following year (for the prior tax year).

list.title: Catch-up Contributions:
list.snippet: Individuals 50 and older can make additional catch-up contributions to their Roth IRA.

list.title: Roth Conversions:
list.snippet: If you exceed the income limits for Roth IRA contributions, you may still be able to convert traditional IRA funds to a Roth IRA.

related_questions.question: What are the rules for contributing to a Roth IRA?

text_blocks.snippet: To contribute to a Roth IRA in 2025, you generally need earned income and your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) must be below certain limits. For single filers, the limit is $150,000, and for joint filers, it's $236,000. There's no age limit, and you can contribute up to $7,000, or $8,000 if you're 50 or older.

list.snippet: Earned Income: You must have taxable compensation to contribute to a Roth IRA.
MAGI Limits: Your MAGI, which is your adjusted gross income plus certain deductions, determines your contribution eligibility.
Contribution Limits: For 2025, the maximum you can contribute is $7,000, or $8,000 if you're age 50 or older.
No Age Limit: You can contribute to a Roth IRA at any age as long as you have earned income and meet the MAGI requirements.
No Deduction: Unlike traditional IRAs, Roth IRA contributions are not tax-deductible.
Tax-Free Withdrawals: Qualified withdrawals of contributions and earnings in retirement are generally tax-free.
Tax Filing Deadline: You have until the tax filing deadline to make contributions for the previous tax year.
Single Filers: If your MAGI is below $150,000, you can contribute the full amount.
Joint Filers: If your MAGI is below $236,000, you can contribute the full amount.
Phased Out: If your MAGI is above these limits but still within certain ranges, your contribution limit may be reduced or eliminated.

text_blocks.snippet: A single person with a MAGI of $140,000 can contribute the full $7,000 (or $8,000 if 50 or older). A married couple filing jointly with a MAGI of $220,000 can also contribute the full amount. However, if a single person's MAGI is $160,000, their contribution limit will be reduced or eliminated.

list.title: 529 Rollover:
list.snippet: Starting in 2024, you may be able to use assets from a 529 plan to contribute to a Roth IRA.

list.title: Recharacterization:
list.snippet: You can recharacterize a Roth IRA contribution as a traditional IRA contribution, but conversions from traditional to Roth IRAs cannot be recharacterized after 2017.

list.title: Excess Contributions:
list.snippet: If you contribute too much, you have until the tax filing deadline to withdraw the excess and any earnings on it, or you may owe a tax on the excess.
